title: The lamb (Exodus 12)
hook: blood on the doorposts, unleavened bread, eaten in haste; Christians call Jesus our Passover

segments.voice: Yesterday, let my people go: bricks without straw, nine plagues, and a heart that kept hardening. Your line was let my people go. Who did you remember among the workers you rarely see? Day three hundred seventy-two.

A meal eaten standing up. Belt fastened, sandals on, walking stick in hand, as if the car's running outside and you might have to leave mid-bite. Roast lamb, flat bread with no yeast because there's no time for dough to rise, bitter herbs. And outside, on the frame of the door, a smear of blood. That's the strangest dinner in the Bible, the night before Israel leaves Egypt. And its name is still in a Catholic church every Easter: on the tall candle, in the songs, in the word priests use for the whole mystery of Christ's death and rising.
screen: `A MEAL EATEN STANDING UP.` → `BLOOD ON THE DOOR FRAME.` → `A NAME STILL HEARD AT EASTER.`

segments.voice: First, the lamb. Each household takes a lamb, a year old, without blemish. On the fourteenth day of the month, at evening, they kill it, and with a bunch of hyssop they brush its blood on the two doorposts and the lintel. Then they eat it, roasted, with unleavened bread, in haste. Second, the night. This is the tenth plague, and the hardest page in Exodus: the death of the firstborn of Egypt. The text doesn't look away from the grief; it says there was a great cry in Egypt, with no house where there was not one dead. But where God sees the blood on the door, God passes over. In Hebrew the feast is called Pesach. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, calls it the Phase, that is, the Passage of the Lord. Third, the remembering. God says: this day shall be a memorial; you will keep it as a feast forever. And Jews still keep Passover every spring at the Seder table, telling this night to their children. Fourth, the word Catholics took from it: Pasch. In Latin and Greek, the same word, pascha, names both Passover and Easter. Jesus ate his last supper at Passover time, and John's Gospel places his death on the day of Preparation for the Passover, when the lambs were being made ready. Paul writes to the Corinthians: "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." At the Easter Vigil, the Easter Proclamation sings that this is the night the true Lamb is slain, whose blood marks the doorposts of believers. The paschal candle, the paschal mystery: every time a Catholic hears that word, it carries a lamb, a door, and a family eating in their traveling clothes.
screen: `A LAMB WITHOUT BLEMISH.` · `WHERE GOD SEES THE BLOOD, GOD PASSES OVER.` · `A MEMORIAL, KEPT FOREVER.` · `CHRIST OUR PASCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one meal with attention. If you have food in front of you, use these two minutes for it. If not, choose your next meal now and plan to slow it down. Look at what's on the plate before you begin. Where did it come from? Who grew it, carried it, cooked it? Take one bite and actually taste it. The Passover meal was eaten in a hurry, but every piece of it meant something, and people have been remembering it ever since. If you pray, you can give thanks before you eat, in your own way or in the Church's grace before meals. If you don't, simply give the food your full attention. The bell holds the time.
Pasch. From Hebrew Pesach, the Passover: the lamb, the blood on the door, the night of leaving. For Catholics, also Easter. Today's word.
Your line: the lord's passover. Today, at one meal, stop before the first bite and remember where it came from. Day three hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, Catholics light the paschal candle and hear the Exsultet, which calls Easter night the night of the true Lamb, and Exodus 12 is read every Holy Thursday at the Mass of the Lord's Supper.

original.note: Hebrew: Passover, from a verb meaning to pass over or spare. Greek and Latin made it pascha, the Church's word for Easter.

trapdoor: what you thought: Passover is a Jewish holiday, Easter a Christian one, and that's that.
what it means: Easter's own name in the Church comes from Passover, and Christians read the lamb on the doorposts as pointing to Christ.
what a scholar hears: Pesach became Greek and Latin pascha; the Douay-Rheims follows the Vulgate's Phase, the Passage of the Lord.

sources.quoted: For Christ our pasch is sacrificed.

notes: Carry 'the lord's passover' follows KJV Exodus 12:11; the DR there reads 'it is the Phase (that is the Passage) of the Lord' — confirm and consider whether the carry should be noted.
The tenth plague is named honestly but briefly ('no house where there was not one dead', 12:30, paraphrased). Keeper may want to review the tone.

John's chronology (Jesus condemned at the sixth hour of the Preparation of the Passover, John 19:14) now phrased as 'John's Gospel places his death on the day of Preparation for the Passover, when the lambs were being made ready'. The Synoptic and Johannine chronologies of the Last Supper differ and are debated; the script avoids saying the Last Supper was itself the Passover meal. Confirm wording.
